d.title: Read a plan from the leaves up, comparing believed against actual
d.caption: **Rows flow upward, so the node at the bottom decides how much work every node above it does** — which is why reading a plan top-down tells you almost nothing. Start at the leaves: what did each scan read, and what did its filter remove? Then at each node ask the only question that matters: **how many rows did the planner believe would flow through here, and how many actually did?** Here the join was estimated at about 4 rows and produced 10. A small gap is normal; a gap of a thousandfold is the cause of the slow query, not a detail of it.

d.title: Three refinements, and the first query never touches the table
d.caption: **The first two rows are the same index and the same seek — the only difference is whether the column you selected happens to be in the index.** When it is, the engine answers from the index alone and the plan says COVERING; when it is not, it seeks and then fetches every matching row from the table. PostgreSQL's INCLUDE adds payload columns to the leaves without putting them in the sort key, which covers the second query too. **A partial index is the cheapest of the three by a wide margin:** indexing only the 5% of refunded rows costs a twentieth of the size and is maintained only when those rows change.

d.title: Two of these come up routinely, and each answers something a B-tree cannot
d.caption: **A B-tree is the right answer to almost everything, and these two cover the cases where it is no answer at all.** A leading-wildcard LIKE cannot use a sorted tree — there is no prefix to bound the search — and **GIN with the trigram extension is the only index that helps it**, by indexing three-character fragments. BRIN is the other: a few kilobytes of per-block minimum and maximum, which lets a range predicate skip whole blocks. **On an append-only log table a B-tree can end up larger than the data it indexes, and BRIN is kilobytes** — but only because the rows arrive in timestamp order.

d.title: An OR needs rows from two places; a NOT asks for everything except
d.caption: **These two fail for opposite reasons.** An OR across two columns needs rows from two different regions of two different indexes, which engines handle by combining the two index results — a bitmap OR, a multi-index OR, an index merge — and where that is unavailable the rewrite is a UNION of two sargable halves. **A negation is harder, because “everything except paid” cannot be read as a range**, so even a selective one may scan. The fix is to give the planner something to seek: name the wanted values in an IN list, or index the exceptions with a partial index.

d.title: Drive the join from the side the predicates shrink most
d.caption: **The filter is on the country, so the join should start from customers and probe outward** — every row that flows upward is then a row somebody asked for. Start from the other end and you scan 800,000 line items, probe orders for each, probe customers for each, and only then discard almost all of it. **The planner chooses this correctly whenever its row estimates are right**, which is why lesson 5.1 comes first: when the estimates are wrong it starts from the wrong side, and the signature in the plan is a large table scanned first with a small one probed per row.

d.title: 561 ms against 0 ms, for numbers that changed only in the current month
d.caption: **The monthly report reads every order and every line item since the beginning, every single run, to produce a few hundred numbers** — and all but one row of that output is identical to yesterday's. Storing those numbers turns the report into a scan of a few hundred rows. A materialised view is the same thing with the database owning the rebuild, which means it can be indexed and refreshed without blocking readers. **The real design question is freshness, and the hybrid is usually the right answer:** the current month live from the base tables, everything older from the summary.

d.title: Same symptom, four signatures, four different fixes
d.caption: **“Slow” is a symptom; the plan carries the signature, and the signature names the fix.** The first two rows look identical from outside the database and have nothing in common inside it: a sequential scan that discarded two million rows wants an index, while a nested loop that ran two million times on an estimate of twelve wants ANALYZE — **no index will fix a bad estimate.** And the third is the one that needs no new object at all: an unsargable predicate is a rewrite, and rewriting `date_trunc` as a half-open range took 820 ms to 12 ms with the existing index.
